articles.description:
I don't enjoy making contact sheets in the darkroom, but I love having them, so Claude and I made an app for it.
I've tried printing "Contact sheets" from apps like Lightroom, etc. but they don't look at all like contact sheets. They're just a boring grid. I wanted something nicer.
I know, it's cheating, but in just a couple of hours I had a native macOS app that generates JPG or PDF contact sheets from a collection of film scans. I drag the scans onto the app,  enter the roll number, camera, film stock, date, and any notes about the roll and I get a reasonable facsimile of a real contact sheet.
Here's the app's UI. Simple and all I need.

I print them on US Letter sized photo paper. There's room on the left to punch holes for the ring binder. Stack them above the matching negative sleeve and it's almost like the real thing, without the hassle.
A printed contact sheet in the binder

I wish I had the energy to make actual contact sheets in the darkroom, but I don't. I'll take this instead.

made EWW his default browswer. That means that whenever he clicks on a URL and certain other links, the link is opened in EWW or—for special links—in another application that runs in Emacs. The point is, all browser activity starts in Emacs, usually in EWW.


Of course, Emacs can’t handle every browsing task so Blais uses the & key in EWW to escape to a “normal” browser. Blais says that EWW suffices for 85–90 percent of his use cases. He has some functions to kick off Emacs apps for MP4, PDF, and other specialized links. Everything else goes to EWW. He’s added a couple of custom bindings for EWW functions he uses a lot but it’s mostly a normal EWW instance.


Blais’ experiment shows that it is possible to almost browse from within Emacs. Sites that rely on JavaScript in an essential way are not going to work of course, and there are still a lot sites that insist on JavaScript so they can enforce the delivery of ads or implement a pay wall. Blais’ method gives us a chance to consider if those sites are worth viewing.

journey from Vim to Emacs. Actually, his journey was from Nano to Emacs by way of Vim. When he first started using Linux, Nano was the default editor and he began with that. Eventually he wanted more power and because Vim seemed more popular in the forums he inhabited, he learned Vim. He really like it and the power that it brought him was an eyeopener.


He experimented with other Vim-like implementations but they didn’t work for him so he stuck with Vim. Eventually he tried Emacs and almost immediately became a convert. Like me, he jumped right in and didn’t try to use Evil or some other Vim emulation. Like many of us, he loved the experience and now wants to do as much as he can in Emacs.


As always, a lot of the action is in the comments. Many said that immigrants from Vim should use Evil because it gives you the best of both worlds: the modal, composable editing commands of Vim and the power and flexibility of Emacs. Others said that Evil induces a sort of cognitive dissonance where neither system is fully in control.


There is, of course, the occasional post proclaiming loudly that Emacs is no good because it uses  Lisp with all those parentheses. The ankle biting aside, the comments offer an intelligent and useful commentary on Sahkopi4’s journey.

articles.description:
hint for those of you who travel and phone home with Emacs. Here’s the situation: you are travelling and log into your home server with SSH and emacsclient. It’s wonderful. Just like being at home except the date/time stamp is wrong. The time and date are whatever your home server thinks they are but you want them to be local time.


The answer is simple. You simply need to change the TZ (timezone) environment variable to reflect your current location. For example, if you’ve travelled to New York (in the US) you would set TZ to “America/New_York”. Emacs, of course, provides a command to do this: (setenv "TZ" "America/New_York").


The zone codes can be a bit opaque so Choi has added a command to the latest Casual suite to set the TZ variable complete with completion. Take a look at his post if you’re interested.
articles.title: Irreal: Setting The Timezone In Emacs

articles.description:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly.
To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.


1

(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")





The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command  casual-timezone-set-tz  that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.


1

M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET





Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs

articles.description:
making his excellent book Let over Lambda available on line and as a PDF. I’ve written about the book several times most importantly here and here but you can search Irreal for “let over lambda” for the the others.


I can’t overemphasize the effect this book had on me. I learned a lot about Lisp and even programming from it. Some people complained that they didn’t like his approach to structuring his Lisp but I never had a problem with it.


The book is about Lisp Macros and the tremendous powers they provide. As an example, Hoyte gives a macro implementation of the Scheme named let construct. There are a lot more things like that in the book.


Let Over Lambda is about Common Lisp but a large portion of it applies to Elisp too. If you’d like to become really good at Elisp, Let Over Lambda is a good resource. As I said, it’s mostly about Common Lisp but a surprising amount carries over to Elisp.


In any event, you can check out the book for free and if you like what you see, you can read the entire book. It is, believe me, well worth your while.
articles.title: Irreal: Let Over Lambda Is Free To Read

articles.description:
org-capture and then create a note1 while the
capture is active (as I'm doing now), you might be very surprised
when you press C-c C-c to finish the note -- it vanishes!
Don't Panic!
In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time
to complete the capture.  Then org-capture adds the item into the
Org file, along with the note.

My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase
  or sentence of the note.  Then I issue the two presses of C-c
    C-c and complete the note at its destination.  I do this
  not only to avoid the "scary missing note" scenario; I also worry
  about leaving work unsaved for any amount of time.  The computers I
  grew up with were prone to crashing at inopportune times, so I
  adopted the motto, "Save Early; save often."  An Org note is
  composed in the *Org Note* buffer, which has no file associated
  with it and therefore is not a good candidate for saving.
1 With C-c C-z (org-add-note)

articles.description:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.


But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.


If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.


The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.


You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.


In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.

The Emacs Carnival topic for November is: Discovery of Emacs Features.
How I Discover Features

Being fairly new in my Emacs journey I find new interesting features all the time, my biggest issue is the time to add them to me workflows. I've been in Emacs long enough now that I dream of being able to move most of my work into it. I open Obsidian to write and wonder why I'm not writing in Emacs. articles.description: When I customize my Emacs, I often utilize hooks. However, when experimenting, I often inadvertently add the wrong thing to a hook – a function I later decide to rename or even a lambda. I have always painstakingly written the correct remove-hook invocation to do it. A few days ago it occurred to me that it would be nice to write an interactive wrapper around remove-hook to make it easier. As usual in such cases, I started with a bit of research to see if someone did something similar already. To my surprise, not only is this a solved problem, but it’s solved in Emacs itself! Apparently, almost six years ago remove-hook was made into a command and you can just M-x it, provide the hook variable name and use autocompletion to decide what to remove from it (including lambdas!). How cool is that?
articles.title: Marcin Borkowski: A tip on removing functions from hooks interactively

articles.description:
Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.”
With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish.
Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file:
Export the Org file to a specified export backend.
View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool.
Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends.
Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee.
Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish

After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player.
Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images.
So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead.  tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but…  The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use.
Things are now faster:

The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash.  I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster…  but gives the wrong result most of the time.  No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini!
So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque.  Sort of:
I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.

It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.

It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.

Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.

Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.

Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.

Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.

rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.

Emacs asks mpv to display it.

Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.

If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.

(repeat 8-9).

Couldn’t be simpler.
articles.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb

articles.description:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.


According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.


Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices,  pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.


The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.


Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.
articles.title: Irreal: BYOK

articles.description:
SAN JOSE, Calif. — "Excuse me, can you move so I can take a photo?" a woman asked me and my friend Adam, referring to the large plaque above us bearing seven photos and an inscription: The Booth That Launched A Multi-Trillion-Dollar Company. How could we deny a fellow pilgrim this humble reliquary? We were all here on this rainy Sunday evening to feel the weight of history settle lightly on our shoulders, and also to have some pancakes. We shuffled out into the otherwise empty room while she took a couple pictures, her solemn bearing occasionally quivering out into a quarter of a grin.
For Steve Jobs, inspiration struck in the garage at 2066 Crist Drive in Los Altos. For Mark Zuckerberg, there was Room H33 at Harvard's Kirkland House Dorm. For Jensen Huang and his Nvidia co-founders, it all started at the Denny's at 2484 Berryessa Road in San Jose, specifically the big booth in the far corner.
Those looking to get closer to the Huang story have few options. You'll have a hard time founding a $4 trillion company, cheating on Jensen Huang's wife, or unwittingly passing on sensitive information to the Chinese government via a mysterious business executive. You have to go back to the beginning. Before Huang was the load-bearing joist propping up the American stock market and an alleged disgrace to the leather jacket community, he was simply a tech worker kicking around Silicon Valley during the first boom. The foundational myth of Nvidia, and by extension Huang, is grounded in the mundane social reality of life in Silicon Valley in some critical ways.
articles.title: Waiting For Jensen

It’s hard to overstate just how absurd we thought the whole thing was, even as we purchased tickets and organized getting to the theater. A Paranormal Activity play. Not a musical, I stressed, though my friends and I kept laughing at how funny that idea seemed. I don’t live in New York and am therefore distant from its many stage sensations, though I’ve been hearing about movies and TV shows, well-known IP, popping up on Broadway for years. 
I remember when the American Psycho musical premiered with Doctor Who (Matt Smith) in the starring role in London in 2013, when they turned The King’s Speech into a play the year before. I was particularly taken with the Once musical as a teenager, though less so with the Moulin Rouge! musical that added more contemporary songs to the jukebox. Last year, Stranger Things: The First Shadow made its way to New York from the UK, a whirlwind of impressive special effects and basically nothing else.
Then Instagram ads for Paranormal Activity populated my feed in late August. I thought maybe a nationwide rescreening was being teased for Halloween. It’s been almost 20 years since the first installment came out, so why not? But I’d missed the tag that read “A New Story Live on Broadway” until a close friend whose critical opinion I value said she was going to see it. I’m an evangelist for the third Paranormal Activity movie, but that’s only because I’m an evangelist for the found-footage form, and that film’s admittedly dumb but effective scares are still some of my favorites.
articles.title: ‘Paranormal Activity’ On Broadway Has Some Good Scares, But Not Much Else

articles.description:
The Detroit Lions beat the reeling New England Patriots, 35-10, in Munich on Sunday. The new NFC North leaders put up almost 500 total yards on offense, with half-German Amon-Ra St. Brown scoring twice on four catches and Jahmyr Gibbs continuing to make his "best player in football" case with 252 total yards and two touchdowns. It was a great win for the Lions, except for one play that simultaneously took out two stars and might have altered the course of the season for both teams.
On New England's first drive of the game, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson got through beleaguered Pats left tackle Will Campbell and took a wide-open angle at quarterback Drake Maye, who couldn't do anything but take a sack and protect the ball. What he couldn't protect, though, was his right ankle, which got caught at an odd angle on the Munich grass. Hutchinson, meanwhile, celebrated his sixth sack of the season, running about 10 yards away and jumping into the air for a fist pump.
That's when everything went to shit. Hutchinson landed awkwardly on his right leg and immediately crumpled to the ground in pain. Detroit's team doctors ran out to check on him as he held onto his right knee. He left the game and eventually returned to the locker room.
articles.title: Aidan Hutchinson Ended The Patriots’ Season, And Then His Own, On One Play

First the San Francisco 49ers were too old to be the best team in football. Then they were too injured to be the best team in football. Now their defense against the lateral is too porous for them to be the best team in football. There's always something with them—the price they must pay for never having actually been the best team in football.
Yet here we are, with them at 8-1 following a Jackson Pollock painting against the Dallas Cowboys, scoring 46 points but allowing 40 and coming within six laterals and two fumbles on the last play of the game from becoming a full-on clown show.
The 49ers have been and still are the most baffling good team in the sport. They give off a pronounced vibe of being indomitable, and sometimes they actually are. Other times, like Sunday, they look like they have too much fun playing with their food. They fell behind 3-0, 10-7 and 16-10, then crushed Dallas for 20 consecutive minutes, and then went back to trading scores until the end of the game, which ended ludicrously enough with a Three Stooges skit that meant lots of work for 14 yards, and left a curious nation to wonder if they aren't just another pretty good team with just enough strengths to hide the flaws that will eventually undo them.
articles.title: The 49ers Will Be The Best Team In Football If They Have To

The Vancouver Canucks won their fourth hockey game of the 50-day-old NHL season Sunday night, but before you grab for your coat and panic-wave at the server to bring your check, this column will not be about the Vancouver Canucks. You deserve better than that. Hell, the Canucks deserve better than that.
But not that much better, because this is about the Toronto Maple Leafs, who just wrapped up a historic 0-6-0 homestand.
There is no city as devoted to its principal sports team than Toronto, based both on size of metropolitan area (7.1 million people) and monomaniacal allegiance (the Blue Jays, Raptors, Argonauts, Marlies, Sceptres, and Tempo are just things our northward friends notice until the lads' next morning skate), and there is no fan base as accustomed to or eager to resume its collective self-flagellation. They have entered their 60th year without either winning or appearing in a Stanley Cup Final, and the customers and their heralds are masters at not only the standard weariness of disappointment but performative fulmination. They love their team, a love which expresses itself as hatred because their team fails them as a function of their existence, and then they find out over time that they actually cut out the middlemen (the Leafs themselves) and end up falling in love with the hatred.
articles.title: The Maple Leafs Are Still Finding New Lows

While prognosticators have been wondering who could be the next school to make an Indiana-type leap into the big leagues, with some already crowning UCLA as the likeliest successor, the Wake Forest Demon Deacons have been quietly developing into something of a budding juggernaut. Those are big words for an ACC program that put up back-to-back 4-8 seasons in 2023 and '24, but I don't think they're totally inaccurate.
In Jake Dickert's first year at the helm of Wake Forest, they went 9-4 with a Mayo Bowl win over Mississippi State. In his second year, they are currently 9-1, with their only loss coming against championship favorite Miami. While they have not exactly gone against a gauntlet, they have dominated in most of their games, particularly in the last six weeks, outscoring their opponents 313-38.
This casualty list added SMU on Saturday when the Demon Deacons crushed the Mustangs 49-7, with 42 points scored in the first half. It was a spanking! Quarterback Gio Lopez accounted for 201 yards and a TD in the air, plus 34 yards and two more TDs on the ground, while the running backs added another 252 yards and four TDs. SMU, which is a good team with a solid record, could do absolutely nothing against these guys. They committed three turnovers and were not able to score until garbage time in the third quarter.
articles.title: Wake Forest Really Kicked Some Ass

articles.description:
Yesterday, good internet friend Baldur Bjarnason shared a series of shorts he made on why he doesn’t use generative AI, and it got me thinking about how much of my career has spent being against things.
Early in my career, I was for web performance and accessibility and building cool things.
But as JavaScript frameworks became increasingly ubiquitous, we saw the things I was for start to degrade rapidly. Sites got slower and harder to use.
articles.title: For and against
